title: Distinguishability Transitions from Global Quantum Snapshots
authors: Catherine McCarthy, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, Romain Vasseur
abstract: Quantum states generated by generic time evolution are locally featureless: local measurements return random outcomes that are identical for all states. However, global snapshots in the computational basis are surprisingly effective at distinguishing between quantum states. We explore the ability of Bayesian classifiers to discriminate between many random quantum states using a small number of measurement outcomes. We identify a phase transition in the ability of the classifier to distinguish between $k$ candidate states with $m$ shots controlled by the variable $x = m / \ln k$, and derive the threshold value $x_c$. We extend our results to low-depth circuits near the onset of anti-concentration, as well as to noisy circuits and phase-random states.
summary: This work analyzes the limits of distinguishing between many random quantum states using only measurements in the computational basis. It finds a sharp phase transition in the success probability of a Bayesian classifier, characterized by a critical scaling variable $x = m / \ln k$. The results provide theoretical benchmarks for quantum state tomography and characterization protocols.
main_problem: The paper investigates the ability of Bayesian classifiers to distinguish between multiple random quantum states using only measurements in the computational basis.
main_result: A phase transition is identified in the distinguishability game, occurring when the ratio of shots to the logarithm of the number of states, $x = m / \ln k$, crosses a critical threshold $x_c$.
method: The analysis uses Bayesian classification theory applied to measurement outcomes (bitstrings) from quantum states, deriving scaling laws and threshold values via saddle-point approximations.
model_or_system: The system involves $k$ candidate quantum states $|\psi_\alphaangle$ generated by generic time evolution (e.g., random circuits) on $N$ qubits. Measurements are restricted to the computational basis, yielding bitstrings $\vec{m}$.
key_observables: Success probability ($P_s$) of the Bayesian classifier, and the critical ratio $x = m / \ln k$.
important_parameters: Number of states ($k$), number of shots ($m$), number of qubits ($N$), and the effective variable $x_{	ext{eff}}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis initially assumes Haar-random states, but extends to noisy and low-depth circuits. The threshold derivation relies on specific asymptotic approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the protocol for state discrimination, showing the success probability $P_s$ transitioning sharply at the critical value $x_c$ when plotted against the effective scaling variable $x_{	ext{eff}}$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of distinguishing states via global snapshots, derives the phase transition scaling $m \sim \ln k$, and then extends this analysis to incorporate noise, low-depth circuits, and specific circuit models (like Clifford circuits) to test the robustness of the transition.
why_interesting: The study connects fundamental concepts of quantum state distinguishability, which is crucial for quantum characterization, to statistical physics concepts like phase transitions, providing a quantitative measure of how much information is encoded in global measurements.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Left: Protocol for distinguishing k random states with m global snapshots. In this setup, an observer is presented with m copies of a random state |ψα⟩with α ∈{0, . . . , k −1} and provided with exact knowledge of all k states. After measuring each site of each of the m copies in the computational basis to obtain a set of bitstrings {⃗mi}, the observer queries a decoder in order to guess the label α. Here we take the decoder to be an optimal Bayesian classifier that outputs the label α associated with the largest probability p({⃗mi}|ψα), where p({⃗mi}|ψj) is computed for all j ∈{0, . . . , k −1} from the Born probabilities associated with the bitstrings {⃗mi}. Right: Decoder success...

FIG. 3. Top: onset of anti-concentration in finite-depth Clifford circuits. The decoder success probability Ps(t, N) decays from one to the expected value for random Clifford circuits Ps(t →∞, N) = 2/3 as the depth t of the circuit is increased. The curves for different system sizes collapse neatly when rescaling by t/ ln(N), indicating that anti-concentration sets in on logarithmic timescales. Bottom: The success prob- ability of an RMPO displays z/η scaling with η the rescaled noise strength in the small-z (deep) limit, and is indepen- dent of η in the large-z (shallow) limit (inset).
